reader.summary: Vietnam's dominant story this week was the signing of a free-trade agreement with four European countries, including Norway and Swiss, a landmark deal that deepens economic ties beyond the existing EU-Vietnam framework. The agreement drew both enthusiasm and criticism: Deutsche Welle and others noted that European governments appeared to prioritize market access while downplaying Vietnam's human-rights record. On the infrastructure front, Vietnam made two major rail announcements: a bet on high-speed rail to transform the economy, and a $3.5 billion non-binding agreement between Maersk and Hateco to build rail freight terminals. The US tariff war, ongoing elsewhere, was reported as boosting Vietnam's coal sector as the country ramps up power generation to feed its factories. Environmental concerns surfaced on multiple fronts: Hanoi moved to curb its iconic street trees, and the government floated remote-work and online-class measures as air quality worsened, while coastal construction in Ho Chi Minh City was reported to be threatening the mangrove belt that shields the city from flooding. In finance, Vietnam announced plans to launch index options next year following an FTSE index upgrade, and its top jeweler rethought diamond buybacks after a sector crisis. A smaller but notable item saw FPT and Denmark's Niels Bohr Institute expand a quantum-talent partnership.

key_events.event: Vietnam signed a free-trade agreement with four European countries including Norway and Switzerland.
Maersk and Hateco signed a non-binding agreement for a $3.5 billion rail freight terminal project in Vietnam.
Vietnam announced a major high-speed rail program aimed at transforming its economy.
Hanoi moved to curb the planting or growth of its iconic street trees amid worsening air quality.
Reuters reported that the US tariff war is fueling a coal boom in Vietnam as the country expands power generation.
Vietnam announced plans to introduce index options next year following its FTSE index upgrade.
Coastal construction projects were reported to be threatening the mangrove forest that protects Ho Chi Minh City.
FPT and Denmark's Niels Bohr Institute announced an expanded collaboration on quantum talent development.

display.eli5:
Vietnam just signed a big trade deal with four European countries, including Norway and Switzerland. Next week, the exciting signing ceremony turns into the boring-but-important part: both sides will publish actual numbers about how much more stuff they will trade, which sectors get lower tariffs, and when the new rules take effect.

At the same time, Vietnam is betting a lot of money on trains. They announced a high-speed rail program and a huge freight terminal project with a shipping company. Next week, those announcements turn into real planning: engineers start studying the routes, the government writes down how much money it will spend, and companies start bidding on construction contracts.

One thing that will probably get louder is the argument about workers' rights. European newspapers and politicians are asking why they are signing a trade deal with a country where workers sometimes struggle to organize. Vietnam will likely send a formal answer, and both sides will keep debating in the press.

What would be a surprise? If Vietnam suddenly announces a new coal power plant or a big renewable energy target because all those US factories moving into Vietnam need a lot more electricity. That would be a plot twist nobody expected from this week's headlines.
